summary: Summarizes the security properties of RSVP, the protocol used to reserve network resources. The analysis aims to build on earlier work and to record what was learned from past security activities around RSVP, and it is informational rather than a new specification.

plainLanguage.summary: RSVP lets you book space on the network, like reserving a table. This memo looks at how to stop strangers from booking tables or cancelling yours.

subtitle: Security mechanisms for reserving network bandwidth and quality of service

tldr.problem: RSVP allows hosts to reserve network bandwidth and quality of service guarantees from routers, but these reservations need protection against spoofing and unauthorized requests.
tldr.mechanism: RSVP provides hop-by-hop integrity checking with keyed hashes, user authentication through policy data elements (supporting Kerberos, X.509, and PGP), and a handshake protocol to recover from message loss or system crashes.
tldr.outcome: These security mechanisms create a chain-of-trust where each router verifies incoming reservation requests and re-protects outgoing ones, though security is only as strong as the weakest router in the path.

today: RFC 4230 is an informational reference that has not been obsoleted. It remains relevant to understanding RSVP's security properties, though RSVP itself is used primarily in carrier networks for traffic engineering via RSVP-TE, which has its own security considerations. The document is useful for analyzing the design choices and trade-offs in QoS signaling protocols.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 4230 summarizes the security properties of RSVP (Resource Reservation Protocol), which allows hosts to request guaranteed quality of service (QoS) from the network. RSVP messages flow through routers, so the protocol must authenticate and protect these reservation requests to prevent unauthorized use or denial-of-service attacks.

The RFC was written as RSVP security considerations were being analyzed for the NSIS working group, which was designing a newer signaling protocol. Rather than repeat security analysis, this RFC summarizes what was learned from RSVP's own security mechanisms and their strengths and weaknesses. Notably, the RFC does not cover RSVP-TE (RSVP for MPLS traffic engineering) or multicast-specific security, both of which lie outside the document's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: This document explains the safety features built into RSVP, the protocol that asks routers to reserve bandwidth. It covers what works well and what doesn't.

sections.title: RSVP Security Mechanisms
sections.content:
RSVP's main security building block is the INTEGRITY object, which protects RSVP messages between neighboring routers (or between a host and router). This object contains a keyed hash (typically HMAC-MD5 or HMAC-SHA-1) computed over the entire message, providing authentication, integrity, and replay protection. Each message carries a 64-bit sequence number to detect replayed packets.

RSVP also supports user authentication through a POLICY_DATA element containing user identity credentials and signatures. Supported credential types include Kerberos V5 tickets, X.509 digital certificates, and PGP certificates. Policy Decision Points (PDPs) in the network can use these credentials to enforce policy-based admission control, allowing or denying reservations based on which user is requesting them. Together, these mechanisms create a chain-of-trust where each router trusts its immediate neighbors but security degrades if any router in the path is compromised.
sections.plainLanguage: RSVP messages are like signed letters: each router checks the signature to make sure it is not forged, then adds its own signature before passing it on. Some messages also include who is asking, so routers can decide if they trust that person.

sections.title: Key Management and Assumptions
sections.content:
RSVP assumes that security associations (shared secrets or keys) are already available before signaling starts. The protocol does not define how to distribute or establish these keys; implementations must support manual key distribution at minimum. This is a significant limitation: key management for a network-wide deployment of RSVP requires a separate infrastructure (such as Kerberos or DNS-based key distribution).

Each security association must have a lifetime and be assigned a unique Key Identifier. Implementers must support overlapping lifetimes so that expired keys do not interrupt ongoing communication. RSVP can use Kerberos to derive session keys, embedding Kerberos tickets in POLICY_DATA, but this adds complexity and requires coordination with a Kerberos realm. The absence of built-in key management means that RSVP's security is only as good as the underlying key distribution system.
sections.plainLanguage: RSVP does not decide how to pass around secret keys; you have to set that up yourself, maybe using a special server that gives out keys. This is the biggest headache when deploying RSVP security.

sections.title: Host and User Authentication
sections.content:
RSVP distinguishes between host authentication and user authentication. Host authentication uses the INTEGRITY object and binds the security association to the host's IP address. This prevents unauthorized hosts from impersonating a known neighbor, but does not identify which user on that host made the request.

User authentication is provided by credentials in the POLICY_DATA element. A Kerberos ticket proves the user to a Kerberos realm. A digital certificate (X.509 or PGP) lets the user sign their reservation request, proving their identity. However, plaintext usernames offer no cryptographic proof. One subtlety is that the Kerberos Authenticator role is played by the RSVP INTEGRITY object: it provides freshness (preventing replay) and proves the user obtained a session key through Kerberos. This coupling means that if a host crashes and loses its sequence numbers, it must request a new Kerberos ticket to prove it is still authorized.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers check two things: who owns the neighboring computer (host auth) and who on that computer is asking (user auth). The second part can use passwords or digital signatures, but passwords are weak unless they are protected by other means.

sections.title: Remaining Vulnerabilities and Limitations
sections.content:
The RFC identifies several weaknesses. First, a chain-of-trust limitation: security is only as strong as the weakest RSVP-aware router in the path. If one router is compromised, it can arbitrarily modify messages and mount attacks that affect all downstream traffic. Second, there is a first-hop problem: a host must trust its first-hop router, and that router must somehow know the host's identity or credentials. If a compromised host or router exists on the local link, it can spoof reservations.

Third, there is a next-hop problem: selecting which router is the next RSVP peer is mostly manually configured, with no standard discovery mechanism. Fourth, authentication at the last hop (between a router and destination host) is weaker than between routers because the destination may not have the RSVP INTEGRITY object protection. Finally, integrating RSVP security with end-to-end IPsec or TLS is not straightforward: the signaling path and data path may differ, and protection must span both layers to be effective.
sections.plainLanguage: The weakest links: any bad router can break everything downstream, you have to trust the router on your local link, and there is no automatic way to discover which router is next. Also, protecting the last hop to your computer is tricky.
